That group’s stack order records which values most recently reached that level. maximum identifies the highest currently occupied level, so popping its final entry satisfies both the frequency priority and the recency tie-break.

Lower-level entries remain as history when a high-level occurrence is removed. They are not duplicates to delete: once a value drops back to that frequency, its earlier level event is again relevant. After popping, decrement the value count; if the highest group empties, move maximum down one level. These updates maintain constant-time operations without stale heap priorities.

At level 2, 7 is more recent than 5 and is popped next.
The next pop removes 5 from level 2, leaving all remaining values at frequency one.
The frequency-one group still records [5,7,4]. Its latest entry is 4, producing pop results [5,7,5,4].

Count each value’s active occurrences. When a push raises its frequency to a level, append it to that level’s stack. Pop from the highest nonempty level; its most recent entry resolves frequency ties. Lower-level records remain ready for later removals.

approach: Track each value’s active frequency and a recency stack for every level.

concept.correctness: A value reaching frequency f records the unmatched push that made its fth active occurrence. Higher levels take priority, so that event remains until the value returns to frequency f. Among all maximum-frequency values, the newest such event is their newest unmatched push. Popping its level stack therefore implements both the frequency and recency rules.
